South Korea's highest-paid math tutor makes $14 million a year, more than Son Heung-min, their most famous footballer. His name is Hyun Woo-jin. He graduated from Stanford's math department in three years and three months. His textbook series, Neuron, sells over a million copies a year. Every November, South Korea pauses for a single nine-hour exam called the Suneung. The Air Force halts training flights. For 35 minutes during the English listening section, no commercial flights can take off or land at Incheon, one of Asia's busiest airports. About 8,000 police officers escort late students on motorcycles with sirens running. Inside that exam, the most consequential questions are called killer questions. They're deliberately designed to fall outside the public school curriculum. They exist to separate the top one percent from everyone else, because that one percent gets into Seoul National, Korea, and Yonsei. The SKY universities that produce around 30% of Korea's top-1,000-company CEOs. Parents can't evaluate the curriculum themselves. They can't reverse-engineer the killer question. So they borrow Hyun Woo-jin's judgment. If your child went through Neuron and still failed, you did what every reasonable parent in the neighborhood does. The fault is your child's, or fate's. Not yours. That's what's actually being sold. Not math. Certainty. Korean households spent 29.2 trillion won on private tutoring in 2024, an all-time record, even as the school-age population dropped another 1.5%. A country is, in a measurable sense, choosing not to exist in order to keep paying for that certainty.

Braised Chicken Legs with Rice, Potatoes & Veggies🍗 Ingredients * 1 package chicken drumsticks (6–7 pieces) * 1-2 tbsp olive oil * 1 tsp salt * 1 tsp black pepper * 2 tsp garlic powder * 2 tsp onion powder * 2 tsp paprika * ½ tsp cumin * 1 jalapeño, diced * ½ red onion, diced * 1 tbsp sun-dried tomato paste * 1 tbsp @Loisa sofrito * 5–6 garlic cloves, minced * 4 cups chicken stock * 1 (8 oz) can tomato sauce * Small potatoes, halved (about 10–12 baby potatoes) * 1 zucchini, diced * Cooked white rice, for serving (let me know if you guys want my rice recipe) Instructions: 1. Clean the chicken with vinegar, then pat completely dry with paper towels. 2. Season the chicken with the salt, pepper, garlic powder, onion powder, paprika, and cumin. Toss until evenly coated. 3. Heat the olive oil in a large Dutch oven or deep skillet over medium-high heat. 4. Brown the chicken for 2–3 minutes per side until golden. It doesn’t need to be cooked through. Remove and set aside. 5. In the same pot, add the diced jalapeño and red onion. Cook for about 5 minutes until softened. 6. Stir in the sun-dried tomato paste and cook for 30 seconds. 7. Add the Loisa Sofrito and minced garlic. Cook for 1 minute until fragrant. 8. Pour in the chicken stock and tomato sauce, stirring to combine. Bring to a gentle boil. 9. Return the chicken to the pot. Reduce the heat to low, cover, and simmer for about 1 hour, or until the chicken is fall-apart tender and the sauce has reduced. 10. About 20 minutes before the chicken is done, add the halved potatoes and diced zucchini. Continue simmering until the potatoes are fork-tender and the zucchini is cooked. 11. Serve over fluffy white rice and spoon plenty of the sauce over the top. #chickenlegs #braised #onepotmeals #cookwithme

these 3 learning methods made me first in my class, and can help you learn anything 10x quicker: 1. interleaving don't study one topic for three hours straight, if you have multiple topics to study, spend a pomodoro (25-50 minutes) on each subject. peformance will feel worse individually, but retention and transfer improves.  2. error journal do NOT focus on what you're good at. focus on your mistakes and what you could be doing better. log everytime you get a practice problem wrong, solve it, write a short sentence on what you did wrong/how you fixed it, and review the whole journal later. high peformers study mistakes more than successes.  3. learning through creating don't just learn a subject and leave as that, i'm sure you know how easily that information gets forgotton over years. create something with it. e.g. if you're learning how to program, code a project. If you're learning math, make your own math problems. It’s no secret that my time in medicine almost killed me. - And I think the biggest reason why (more than the hours and the exhaustion) was this idea that we’re supposed to accept all of it with a smile. With gratitude. As if the system is doing us a FAVOUR. The 14-hour shifts, 7 days in a row. The mental overwhelm from having urgent 7 tasks competing for your attention. The constant anxiety and fear of making the wrong mistake that could cost a life. The superiors who look straight through you. And then, when you say anything about it, you’re met with: “Oh but how LUCKY are you to be a doctor?” “You’re saving lives, why would you want to do anything else?” That’s the part that really f*cking broke me 😞 I ended up leaving medicine because I just couldn’t take it any longer. And even then, I felt so guilty because of this exact attitude. I thought I was weak, for choosing not to suffer for such a prestigious career. But now that I’ve built a career that I genuinely LOVE and ENJOY every single day… I’ve learnt that suffering SHOULDN’T be a rite of passage. It’s not what makes you a good doctor. It’s not what makes you “worthy” of the title. And it was NEVER supposed to be the price you pay for a career that you love. The more that we say this out loud, and support others who are brave enough to say it too, the louder that calling gets. So, are you with me? 🙏🏽 - P.S. 📚 Study to understand, not to cram. If you only memorize, you’ll forget after the exam. When you understand why something works, your brain remembers it longer and you can answer unfamiliar questions with confidence. 🔁 Use Active Recall instead of re-reading. After studying a topic, close your notes and try to explain everything you remember. Every time you struggle to recall something, your brain becomes stronger at retrieving that information. ⏳ Revise with Spaced Repetition. Don’t read a topic once and abandon it. Revise it after 1 day, 3 days, 7 days, and again later. This tells your brain the information is important and prevents forgetting. 🗣️ Teach the topic like you’re a lecturer. If you can’t explain it in simple words, you don’t understand it well enough. Teaching exposes the exact areas you need to work on. 📝 Practice with past questions early. Past questions reveal how lecturers think and the pattern of exams. They also train you to apply knowledge instead of just recognizing it in your notes. 🎯 Spend more time on your weak areas. Most students keep reading their favorite subjects because it feels comfortable. Top students improve faster because they deliberately fix their weakest topics first. 📵 Remove distractions while studying. Every notification breaks your concentration, and your brain needs several minutes to regain deep focus. One uninterrupted hour is more valuable than three distracted hours. ✍️ Create short summary notes. After every study session, write the key ideas on one page. During revision, you’ll review your summaries instead of hundreds of pages. 😴 Protect your sleep. Sleep is when your brain organizes and stores what you’ve learned. Reading all night and sleeping very little often leads to poor recall in the exam hall. 🚀 Be consistent, not extreme. You don’t need to study 12 hours in one day. Studying with focus for 2–3 hours consistently over weeks will outperform last-minute cramming almost every time. 🏆 Final Lesson: The smartest classmate isn’t always the one with the highest IQ. More often, it’s the one with the best study system, the most consistency, and the discipline to keep improving every single day. #studentmotivation #studytok #motivation #discipline #howtostudy
